introduction: A revelation is a spring. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá uses the image constantly, and these readings gather what he and Bahá’u’lláh do with it. Spring returns; last year’s is a story and this year’s is here. The same sun and rain make one tree blossom and leave another bare. Each spring has its summer, autumn and winter, and no sensible person says one spring was enough for all time. The days of the nightingale are short, so “seize the time.” And the present winter of the world is the sign that spring is close. The Hebrew prophets and psalms are full of the same weather: Isaiah’s desert in blossom, Hosea’s dew, Joel’s latter rain, the Song of Songs. So are the Qur’án’s verses on the dead earth revived, and the Gospels on seed, harvest, bridegroom and the light that is “yet a little while” with you. English poetry adds Chaucer’s April, Herbert, Shelley, Tennyson and Hopkins. The contrasts are Eliot’s cruel April, the Preacher’s “no new thing,” Wordsworth’s dawn that failed, and the three texts usually read as closing the series: Hebrews, Jude and the Seal of the Prophets.
questions: “Last year’s springtime is past and all that thou mayest say or hear about it is but a story.” What is the difference between a faith that is a story of a past spring and one that is a present spring? How would you tell from outside?
The same rain falls on the green tree and the dry one. What, in the readings and in Hebrews and the Qur’án, makes the difference between them? Is it within a person’s power?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá says no one would call one spring “sufficient for all time.” How would you put that to a Christian who holds to “the faith once delivered,” or a Muslim who holds to the Seal of the Prophets?
“Seize the time.” Compare Herrick’s rosebuds, Brutus’s tide and Jesus’ “the night cometh.” What exactly is to be seized, and how?
Eliot’s April is cruel, and Hopkins watches the spring and asks for rain on his own roots. What do the readings offer to those who are disturbed by renewal or untouched by it?
Wordsworth and Dickens both remember an age that felt like spring and was also terror. What signs do the readings give for telling a real spring from a mood?

outside.why: “Spring returneth over and over again, and setteth up a great new commotion.” The Song of Songs: lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone; the flowers appear on the earth; the time of the singing of birds is come.
A psalm on the power at work in every spring: thou sendest forth thy spirit, they are created: and thou renewest the face of the earth.

Spring as bounty and commotion. T. S. Eliot opened The Waste Land in 1922 with a spring nobody wanted: April is the cruellest month, breeding lilacs out of the dead land, stirring dull roots with spring rain. Why might a renewal be feared by those it comes to?

“Last year’s springtime is past and all that thou mayest say or hear about it is but a story.” God in Isaiah: remember ye not the former things; behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth.

Appreciate this year’s spring. Jesus observed how people actually respond: no man having drunk old wine straightway desireth new: for he saith, The old is better. What makes last year’s story easier to love than this year’s spring?
The virtues “are renewed in every Dispensation.” Jesus on the renewal: neither do men put new wine into old bottles; they put new wine into new bottles, and both are preserved.
He that sat upon the throne said, Behold, I make all things new.
“Gradually whatsoever is latent … shall appear,” for now is only the beginning of its growth. Jesus: first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear.
“Strive that … fruits may appear from the tree of your being.” The first psalm: like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season.

Plants grow by the spring’s gifts and “are unaware of their privilege.” Jeremiah found that the birds do better than people: the stork in the heaven knoweth her appointed times; but my people know not.

The same spring: the green tree blossomed, the dry one “remained deprived.” The Letter to the Hebrews: the earth which drinketh in the rain and bringeth forth herbs receiveth blessing; but that which beareth thorns and briers is rejected.
The Qur’án: as for the good land, its vegetation cometh forth by permission of its Lord; while as for that which is bad, only evil cometh forth.

The four seasons, and the Manifestations as “the divine springtime.” The promise after the flood: while the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter shall not cease.
The Preacher: to every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven.
“Rain-laden clouds and musk-scented breezes.” The Qur’án reads spring as a sign in the same way: He sendeth the winds as tidings heralding His mercy.
The teaching of a Prophet as spring weather. Moses, in his last song: my doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew.
Hosea: he shall come unto us as the rain, as the latter and former rain unto the earth.
When the Holy Spirit appears “the world is revived.” A psalm for the just king: he shall come down like rain upon the mown grass.
Joel, who goes on to promise the pouring out of the Spirit: be glad then, ye children of Zion: for he hath given you the former rain moderately, and the latter rain.
“In every age and cycle He hath … recreated all things.” Krishna in the Bhagavad Gita: when Righteousness declines, I rise, from age to age.

Cycles are “inaugurated, concluded, and renewed.” The Letter to the Hebrews opens with what reads as a last word: God, who at sundry times spake in time past by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son. How do the readings understand a “last” that is followed by another spring?

The Qur’án: Muḥammad is the messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets. Most Muslims read this as the end of prophecy. What does the image of returning seasons ask them to reconsider, and what does it leave in place?
“The circle of existence is the same circle; it returns.” Shelley: the world’s great age begins anew, the golden years return, the earth doth like a snake renew her winter weeds outworn.

Cycles came before this one and left no trace. The Preacher drew a weary conclusion from the same fact: there is no new thing under the sun. What keeps ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s cycles from being mere repetition?
Every achievement ends; only “the great Cause of the Kingdom” remains. Isaiah: the grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
“Every spring has an autumn.” Hopkins to a child crying over falling leaves, in a poem he called Spring and Fall: sorrow’s springs are the same.
In the winter people “become spiritless and withered.” George Herbert, after such a season in himself: who would have thought my shrivel’d heart could have recover’d greennesse?

Autumn and winter set in, and then the spring. Jesus on what the dead season is for: except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.

No one of intelligence would say last year’s spring is “sufficient for all time.” The Letter of Jude says something close to that of the faith: contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints. What in a religion is given once, and what must come again?
“It is the day of the wedding feast, the springtime.” Jesus of his own days: can the children of the bridechamber mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them?
The outward spring comes once a year; the spiritual spring far more rarely. A psalm on God’s calendar: a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past.
The vernal showers “will not rain forever.” Jesus: yet a little while is the light with you. Walk while ye have the light.
Isaiah: seek ye the Lord while he may be found, call ye upon him while he is near.
“Seize the time, therefore, ere the glory of the divine springtime hath spent itself.” Jesus: I must work while it is day: the night cometh, when no man can work.
Brutus in Julius Caesar: there is a tide in the affairs of men, which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune.

Seize the time. Herrick’s advice sounds the same and aims elsewhere: gather ye rosebuds while ye may, old time is still a-flying. What is the difference between seizing a day for oneself and seizing the day Bahá’u’lláh means?

The Nightingale will fly, and “its melody be heard no more.” Keats heard a nightingale that seemed to outlast every listener: thou wast not born for death, immortal Bird! What is it that departs when a Manifestation departs, and what remains?
“Know the value of these days, for union is not always possible.” Jesus wept over a city that had not: thou knewest not the time of thy visitation.
Fruits that “in other seasons … cannot be found.” Jeremiah gives the cry of those who waited: the harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved.
“What regret and remorse.” Jesus’ story of ten girls with lamps, five of whom were away buying oil when the bridegroom came: and the door was shut.
“The withered earth brought forth immortal blooms.” Isaiah: the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose.
“There came tidings of great joy.” The phrase is Luke’s: behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people.
Meadows adorned and fountains made to flow by a “ceaseless downpour.” A harvest psalm: thou visitest the earth, and waterest it; thou crownest the year with thy goodness.

The breezes and showers of Farvardín, the first month of the Persian spring. The best-known April in English also sets people moving toward a holy place: whan that Aprill with his shoures soote … thanne longen folk to goon on pilgrimages.

“Soon the whole world, as in springtime, will change its garb.” Isaiah: as the garden causeth the things that are sown in it to spring forth; so the Lord God will cause righteousness and praise to spring forth before all the nations.
“The new year hath appeared.” Tennyson’s bells: ring out the old, ring in the new; ring out the false, ring in the true.
After the spring “all phenomena become imbued with the life of a new creation.” Paul: if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.
The Qur’án: thou seest the earth barren, but when We send down water thereon, it doth thrill and swell and put forth every lovely kind of growth.
“The trees of human souls become green and flourishing.” Hosea: I will be as the dew unto Israel: he shall grow as the lily.
“He is the Divine Spring which comes after the long winter.” Zacharias’ song: the dayspring from on high hath visited us, to give light to them that sit in darkness.
“The earth of souls was stirred.” The Qur’án: seest thou not how Allah sendeth down water from the sky and then the earth becometh green upon the morrow?
“This is the Day of rejoicing.” A psalm: this is the day which the Lord hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it.

“The age of estrangement has passed. The century of friendship has arrived.” Wordsworth remembered feeling the same in 1789: bliss was it in that dawn to be alive. He lived to see that dawn turn to terror and war. What distinguishes the spring announced here from the false dawns of history?
The Cause is in its springtime: “open, then, the ear of understanding.” Jesus’ parable of the season: a sower went forth to sow, and the yield depended on the ground.
“A New Cycle, a New Age, a New Century, a New Time and a New Year.” The psalms: O sing unto the Lord a new song.

Naw-Rúz, when the Sun “shone forth in the heaven of glory.” FitzGerald’s Omar Khayyám opens with a Persian sunrise: Wake! For the Sun has scattered into flight the stars before him from the field of night.
The sun at the vernal point bestows “a new grace and a potent spirit.” Malachi: unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings.
“This cycle is eternal.” The Preacher: the sun also ariseth, and the sun goeth down, and hasteth to his place where he arose.
At the equinox “the sun illumines equally the whole earth,” a symbol of the divine messenger. Jesus on the Father: he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good.
“That which had withered is restored to freshness and life.” Hopkins: nature is never spent; there lives the dearest freshness deep down things.
“This is the spring season of God.” The Qur’án: look, therefore, at the prints of Allah’s mercy: how He quickeneth the earth after her death.

A “wonderful vibrant energy” everywhere. Hopkins looked at just such a spring and felt left out of it: birds build, but not I build; mine, O thou lord of life, send my roots rain. What do the readings say to someone who sees the spring and does not feel it?
“A new order and condition is established.” Tennyson’s dying Arthur: the old order changeth, yielding place to new, and God fulfils himself in many ways.
“The weeping of the clouds … is followed by the laughter of rose gardens.” A psalm: they that sow in tears shall reap in joy.
Longfellow: into each life some rain must fall, some days must be dark and dreary.
“The April showers of the mercy of the All-Merciful have poured down.” Ezekiel: I will cause the shower to come down in his season; there shall be showers of blessing.
Isaiah: I will pour water upon him that is thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground; and they shall spring up as willows by the water courses.
“The surface of the earth was transformed.” John’s vision: I saw a new heaven and a new earth.
“The time for strolling in the rose garden has begun.” Wordsworth thought such a walk a teacher: one impulse from a vernal wood may teach you more of man than all the sages can.
The “new saplings that were planted by the divine hand of training.” A psalm’s picture of a blessed household: thy children like olive plants round about thy table.
Children as “tender seedlings” and “fresh saplings.” Jesus’ smallest seed: when it is grown, it is the greatest among herbs, and becometh a tree.
“In the springtime of youth.” Ecclesiastes: remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth.
Breezes, clouds, sun and trees are all read as grace. Pope on the one presence in them: warms in the sun, refreshes in the breeze, glows in the stars, and blossoms in the trees.
The breezes of the divine springtime “have made meadow and plain verdant.” Paul on who does the growing: I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.
“The spring rain giveth life to the black earth.” Isaiah makes the comparison explicit: as the rain cometh down and watereth the earth, so shall my word be.
The present state of the world is winter, “but the spring … is bound to come.” Shelley: O Wind, if Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?

Winter now, spring coming. Dickens wrote of 1775 that it was both at once: it was the spring of hope, it was the winter of despair. Is every age both, or do the readings mean something a historian could date?
“Wait until spring and then all is gladness.” Habakkuk learned to rejoice before it came: although the fig tree shall not blossom, yet I will rejoice in the Lord.
“Soon shall we see the signs of the coming of the spring.” Jesus: when the fig tree’s branch is yet tender, and putteth forth leaves, ye know that summer is nigh.
The progress of the Cause is like early signs: a tree in leaf here, a bush in flower there. Jesus: lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest.

The Faith advances by “rhythmic pulsations” of crisis and victory. James: the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain.

quran-winds-as-tidings-heralding-his-mer.text: And He it is Who sendeth the winds as tidings heralding His mercy, till, when they bear a cloud heavy (with rain), We lead it to a dead land, and then cause water to descend thereon and thereby bring forth fruits of every kind. Thus bring We forth the dead. Haply ye may remember.

quran-water-from-the-sky-and-the-earth-b.text: Seest thou not how Allah sendeth down water from the sky and then the earth becometh green upon the morrow? Lo! Allah is Subtile, Aware.

hebrews-earth-which-drinketh-in-the-rain.text: For the earth which drinketh in the rain that cometh oft upon it, and bringeth forth herbs meet for them by whom it is dressed, receiveth blessing from God: But that which beareth thorns and briers is rejected, and is nigh unto cursing; whose end is to be burned

joel-former-rain-and-the-latter-rain.text: Fear not, O land; be glad and rejoice: for the Lord will do great things. Be not afraid, ye beasts of the field: for the pastures of the wilderness do spring, for the tree beareth her fruit, the fig tree and the vine do yield their strength. Be glad then, ye children of Zion, and rejoice in the Lord your God: for he hath given you the former rain moderately, and he will cause to come down for you the rain, the former rain, and the latter rain in the first month

matthew-children-of-the-bridechamber.text: Can the children of the bridechamber mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them? but the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken from them, and then shall they fast

psalm-turn-again-our-captivity-as-the-st.text: Turn again our captivity, O Lord, as the streams in the south. They that sow in tears shall reap in joy. He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him
